Creating Custom Controls

In this guide, we'll create a UIElement-derived control with a caption, active state and keyboard callback. We'll then use it in both C# and MXML.

Prerequisites

  • A .NET 10 project referencing MelonUI.
  • The binding generator referenced by the project containing your annotated fields. See Binding Generator for setup.
  • A basic understanding of the UIElement properties and the ConsoleBuffer.

1. Create the Control Class

Add the following Badge class to your project:

Understanding the Code

  • partial class: Allows the binding generator to add properties to the class.
  • Binding Fields: Generate Caption, Active and OnActivated. These properties use the base binding and invalidation behavior.
  • ContentRect: Gives the usable area inside the border. A bordered control with Height=3 has one content row.
  • RenderContent: Draws the active marker and caption, clipping by text elements so long text does not overwrite the border.
  • TryHandleKey: Toggles Active on Enter, calls OnActivated, and returns true to mark the key as handled.

2. Add the Control in C#

The generated setters already invalidate the element. You do not need to call Invalidate again after assigning Caption or Active. State that is not handled by those setters should invalidate the control explicitly.

3. Use the Control in MXML

Register the assembly and namespace before compiling the page:

App.Save is a public parameterless method on your registered backend. If two types have the same short name, use a CLR XML namespace prefix. For this example that would be xmlns:docs="clr-namespace:MelonUI.Docs;assembly=MelonUI.DocsExamples", followed by docs:Badge. Replace the assembly name with the name of your own assembly.

If the control needs constructor arguments, register a factory through CompilerOptions.Factories.

4. Manage Subscriptions and Resources

A control may be removed and reused without being disposed. Subscribe to window events while attached and remove those subscriptions when detached:

Stop or cancel window-specific work on detach, while keeping the object reusable. DisposeCore is for final resource cleanup. Keep lifetime methods synchronous and avoid throwing from them during cleanup.

5. Build and Test

A control should be checked in more than its initial layout. Test the following:

  • Small Sizes: One row, no content area, clipped layouts, nested parents and repeated resizing.
  • Input: Modifier keys, disabled/hidden/locked state, unhandled keys, focus navigation and modals.
  • Bindings: Property changes, callbacks, detach/reattach, document replacement and disposal.
  • Drawing: Borders, transparent backgrounds, Unicode text and cache invalidation.
  • Lifetime: Repeated reuse without duplicate subscriptions or abandoned background work.

Custom containers also need to lay out and draw their children. If the standard page behavior is enough, derive from or use MUIPage instead.
